title: The paradox at the core of the AI revolution: The faster we innovate, the slower we grow
source_used: Fortune (full text from the main session's fulltext copy)
key_facts: Ming Lu, a senior advisory partner at KKR and former executive chairman of KKR Asia Pacific, argues in a Fortune commentary that digital technology spreads fast among consumers but has not lifted productivity growth; he calls this the Innovation Paradox.
He cites McKinsey's 2026 State of AI survey: 88% of organisations use AI in at least one function, but only 6% qualify as 'high performers' with more than 5% EBIT impact, unchanged from 2025.
He says only 21% of AI adopters have redesigned workflows end to end, and the 6% who succeed are three times more likely to have done so.
He puts consumer AI use at 53% of US adults about three years after ChatGPT's launch, against 10% of enterprise AI in productive deployment.
He says 36 S&P 500 AI companies make up 45% of the index's market value; over three years the S&P 500 returned 76%, or 32% without AI stocks.
He cites a Writer 2026 survey of 2,400 global leaders: 79% report challenges in AI adoption and 54% of C-suite executives say adoption is 'tearing their company apart'.

He blames company overhead and slow organisational change, using his own 'Combined Overhead Ratio' (government spending, corporate selling and administrative costs, and compliance costs), not weak technology.
His conclusion: history suggests adoption takes over ten years, often decades, and real impact comes only when AI is adopted deeply inside firms and broadly across large sectors.
quote_evidence: I call this the Innovation Paradox: the faster we innovate, the slower we grow.
McKinsey’s 2026 survey found that 88% of organizations use AI in at least one function, but a mere 6% qualify as “high performers” achieving more than 5% EBIT impact—unchanged from 2025.
The Innovation Paradox persists not because technology fails to advance, but because institutions fail to adapt.
why_it_matters_hint: A KKR partner argues that AI's payoff for the wider economy depends on companies redesigning how they work, which history suggests takes a decade or more.
notes: Opinion piece: Fortune states the views are the author's. The statistics are the author's citations of McKinsey and Writer surveys and his own overhead metric; not independently checked here. Keep opinion separate from fact in the entry.
